items.title: How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest
items.summary:
On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone. Days went by, and officials assumed he was dead. And then, six days after vanishing, he crawled on his hands and knees out of the Khumbu Icefall toward Base Camp, where he was rescued by camp workers.

Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak. And the 57-year-old wasn’t supposed to have been on Everest’s highest slopes in the first place.

He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures. The company had just two paying clients for the 2026 season: Chris Thrall, a British ex-Royal Marine, and Mariusz Chmielewski, a plumber from Poland.

But late in the expedition, Hillary Dawa was asked to guide Thrall up the mountain, after Himalayan Traverse Adventures sent one of its experienced climbing Sherpas home.

“I was only supposed to be a cook, but they offered me 10,000 Rupees a day to climb with the clients,” Hillary Dawa told Outside . “I didn’t even want to go to Everest this year.”

Outside reached out to Himalayan Traverse Adventures but did not receive answers for this story. Hillary Dawa said company management believed Thrall was incapable of making it above Camp IV. But Thrall eventually reached the summit. Hillary Dawa and Chmielewski turned back before the top and retreated to Camp IV. On the descent, the company’s other climbing Sherpa sped ahead down the peak,…
items.t: How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest

items.title: Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.
items.summary:
“WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.

The NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod. A nearly full moon illuminates her curly hair, with her tent and a field of scraggly creosote bush behind her. The Big Bend National Park campsite is large enough to sleep eight people, but it’s just the two of us here tonight. Even at 10 P.M., the temperature hovers in the mid-70s. It’s already past my bedtime, but Koch and I came to the park to witness what happens in the sky after dark.

“If you look to the lower left, there’s a dark spot, almost like a mole. Carroll Crater is a little up to the left of that,” Koch says as I bend down to look through the lens, the dark splotches of the moon suddenly massive and detailed to my right eye.

Koch peers through a moonscope (Photo: Abigail Wise) 
 Koch and the other three astronauts on the 2026 Artemis II mission named Carroll Crater after colleague and mission commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. Mission specialist Koch, Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen made history in April 2026 when they completed a ten-day-long mission around the moon, traveling a record-setting 252,757 miles from Earth, livestreaming the event, and going viral along the way. It made Koch the first woman to travel around the moon, adding another record to her list, which also includes the longest spaceflight by a woman (328 days throughout 2019 and 2020), and embarking on the first all-women…
items.t: Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.

items.title: What We Learned When Sabastian Sawe Finally Broke the 2-Hour Marathon
items.summary:
In the early 2010s, the idea of breaking two hours in the marathon went from pipe dream to attainable goal. For the first decade of the new millennium, the world’s top distance runners had been chipping away at it. Paul Tergat first breached the 2:05 barrier with his 2:04:55 mark at the 2003 Berlin Marathon. Haile Gebrselassie ran 2:03:59 at the same race in 2008, and by 2014, Dennis Kimmetto held the record with a 2:02:57, less than seven seconds per mile away from sub-two.

Like the four-minute mile, first toppled by Roger Bannister in Oxford, England, in 1954, the two-hour marathon is an enticing target. It’s an even number in a popular event. It’s easy to describe, and therefore easy to market. Perhaps that’s why Nike decided to pour millions of dollars into their Breaking2 project, starting in 2016, bringing Eliud Kipchoge within 30 seconds of the barrier on May 6, 2017, in an exhibition race on the F1 track in Monza, Italy.

After that much-watched effort, Kipchoge became the torchbearer for breaking two hours. His next attempt in 2019 came with a perfectly flat looped course, a roster of pacers blocking the wind, controlled nutrition on a controlled course, and a finishing time of 1:59:40. Kipchoge showed the world that sub-two was possible. He made history. But he didn’t do it in a race.

It would take a special set of circumstances to see the result in a record-eligible setting. An elite athlete would need the right training, the right weather conditions, the right competition. The previous nine times the world record had been set, these circumstances came…
items.t: What We Learned When Sabastian Sawe Finally Broke the Two-Hour Marathon

items.title: Now 40, Alex Honnold Must Juggle Climbing with Fatherhood and Fame. It Isn’t Always Easy.
items.summary:
Alex Honnold , holding a bowl of Cheerios in one hand and a spoon of peanut butter in the other, stands at a kitchen island between his two giggling daughters and scowls at the clock. Here it is, barely 8 A.M., and he is already running late. Honnold quickly calculates the jam-packed agenda for what will be his family’s final summer day at their vacation cabin in South Lake Tahoe. Valuable seconds tick by.

After breakfast, Honnold must drop the girls off at preschool and then link up with a team of photographers and videographers at Pie Shop , a climbing crag on the other side of town. There, he will pose for a magazine cover shoot while clinging to rotund granite boulders, before speeding back to the cabin to have lunch with his aunt, who is visiting from Idaho. After that, Honnold will pack his luggage for an upcoming family trip to Italy. Finally, the Honnolds will host a few friends and neighbors for a goodbye barbecue.

The breakneck schedule is made more challenging by lingering jet lag from a recent trip to London, where Honnold delivered a motivational speech at an event hosted by his longtime sponsor the North Face.

“These days I feel like a ping-pong ball,” Honnold says. More seconds tick by.

Honnold will have to complete much of today’s agenda while answering the prying questions of a pesky journalist—me. Back in January, Honnold’s Netflix special Skyscraper Live thrust him into millions of living rooms across the planet, elevating him to a loftier stratosphere of fame. At Outside , we named Honnold an Outsider of the Year, in part, for bringing the grandeur…

items.title: Jimmy Chin on His New Mount Everest Film and Latest Book
items.summary:
In spring 2026, Jimmy Chin flew to Nepal. It was his 15th trip to the Greater Ranges over 25 years spent on expeditions to climb and photograph its snow-covered giants. The trip was a departure from the high-octane sufferfests he’s often done, and it also marked a different type of first: the first time he brought his kids, Marina (12) and James (10), along. Showing them the mountains that have inspired him for decades, and often pulled him away from them for months at a time, was memorable for Chin.

Together, they made their way to Everest Base Camp, stopping in the tiny villages that populate the roadless Khumbu Valley. When they crawled into their tents at 17,598 feet, they were proud of themselves.

Outside Phortse, a small village in Sagarmatha National Park, a helicopter dropped off a special guest who’d come to say hi: Jim Morrison. Morrison hadn’t wanted to miss the kids’ first trip to Nepal, and they were shocked to see him walking toward them on the trail. In town, they went to the Khumbu Climbing Center , where Nepali climbers and high-altitude workers train to operate safely in the big mountains, to hang with Sherpa friends and their families, and to pick up their guide, Pemba Sherpa (Sharwa).

Twenty years earlier, Chin had encountered a then 15-year-old Pemba for the first time in that exact spot. It was just a few years after the center had opened, and he and the legendary mountaineer Conrad Anker were on the way to climb Cholatse. “I really encouraged his photography and filmmaking,” said Chin.

items.title: Feeling Tension in the Lower-Body After Your Latest Adventure? Do This Simple Stretch.
items.summary:
I often sing the praises of the Warrior I yoga pose (a.k.a. Virabhadrasana I) to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it.

In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West.

The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I or Warrior I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches.

What Are the Hip Flexors and What Do They Do? 
 The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.)

items.title: 3 Dead in Plane Crash on Remote North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park
items.summary:
Three people are dead after a plane crashed on the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park on November 15, 2026.

Authorities have not released the identities of the people aboard the plane or details about the accident. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the accident, the National Park Service (NPS) wrote in a statement .

According to the NPS, the Grand Canyon Regional Communications Center received a call about a missing Piper Comanche at 11:30 P.M. on November 15. Produced between 1958 and 1972, the Piper Comanche is an older single-engine, low-wing aircraft that typically seats between four and six people.

The Arizona Department of Public Safety conducted an aerial search in the early morning hours of November 16 using infrared and night vision, according to the NPS.

“The aircraft and debris field were located by NPS at approximately 10:15 A.M. on November 16 in the Basin area,” officials said. “There were no survivors.”

The North Rim is an isolated part of the Grand Canyon that sees just about ten percent of the park’s visitors annually. It’s a rugged, higher-elevation area on the Kaibab Plateau that averages about 8,300 feet—roughly 1,000 feet higher than the South Rim. All park amenities on the North Rim are closed November through April, and the road into the park closes in December.

The Arizona Department of Public Safety, Coconino County Search and Rescue, Kane County Search and Rescue, and Air Force Rescue Coordination Center participated in the search efforts.

Since 1986, NPS data show 12 aircraft incidents within Grand Canyon…
